title: Bullet/Flame/Lava-Heat Proof — Overview
description: Bullet/Flame/Lava-Heat Proof (Plasma Amor Grade): Overview. Bullet-resistant clothing stops or slows projectiles with layered high-strength fibers and, for rifle threats, hard armor plates. Soft armor defeats handgun rounds; plates defeat rifle rounds. Flame-resistant clothing chars instead of melting, buying seconds of escape time in flash fire. It does not make the wearer fireproof; it limits burn injury when every second counts. Lava heat is radiant furnace heat: basaltic lava runs 700 to 1200 C and radiates hundreds of kW/m2. Real proximity gear reflects radiant heat for short approaches; nothing wearable survives immersion. Plasma Amor Grade: tri-threat union with the plasma-amor concept layer (labeled).

details: A bullet's kinetic energy is E = 1/2 m v^2. A 9 mm 124-grain round at 360 m/s carries about 518 joules; armor must absorb and spread that energy.
Fibers stop bullets by tensile failure, yarn pull-out, and cone formation: the impact cone widens the loaded area so energy spreads across many yarns.
Ceramic plates defeat rifle rounds by shattering the projectile nose on a hard face, then the composite backer catches the slower fragments.
Energy spreads in time as well as space: each layer strains, breaks, and passes a reduced load onward, which is why layer count maps to threat level.
Heat flux is measured in kW/m2 or cal/cm2-s; a flash fire delivers about 84 kW/m2 (2 cal/cm2-s).
Time to second-degree burn is roughly TPP divided by heat flux: a TPP-12 fabric at 2 cal/cm2-s gives about 6 seconds.

details: Select the threat level first (IIA/II/IIIA soft, III/IV with plates); the threat decides the material stack.
Cut woven aramid or UHMWPE plies to the panel pattern; orient alternating plies 0/90 degrees for balanced strength.

Enclose panels in a water-resistant carrier with plate pockets, then proof-test one panel per lot against the rated threat.
Choose the hazard standard first: NFPA 2112 for flash fire, 1971 for firefighting, F1506 for arc flash.

details: Silk vests in the 1800s and World War I showed layered textiles could slow low-velocity rounds.
Flak jackets of World War II and Korea used nylon to stop fragments, not bullets.
DuPont's Kevlar (1965, Stephanie Kwolek) made practical soft body armor possible in the 1970s.
UHMWPE fibers (Dyneema, 1990s) cut vest weight; ceramics brought rifle protection to wearable plates.
Asbestos cloth was the original heat garment, abandoned once its health cost was proven.
Nomex arrived in the 1960s and dressed race drivers and astronauts within a decade.

details: Match the level to the realistic threat: IIIA covers nearly all handgun duty; plates are for rifle environments.
Fit matters as much as material: gaps at the sides and shoulders are the most common real-world failure.
Weigh the armor: a IIIA vest runs about 1.5 to 2.5 kg; a loaded plate carrier with IV plates can exceed 10 kg.
Check the NIJ compliant-products list; uncertified 'bulletproof' clothing is a marketing claim, not a rating.
Match the standard to the hazard: 2112 for flash fire, 1971 for firefighting, F1506 arc ratings for electrical.
Read the arc rating or TPP number, not the brand: numbers compare, adjectives do not.

description: Bullet/Flame/Lava-Heat Proof (Plasma Amor Grade): Signature concept — future path. Bullet-resistant clothing stops or slows projectiles with layered high-strength fibers and, for rifle threats, hard armor plates. Soft armor defeats handgun rounds; plates defeat rifle rounds. Flame-resistant clothing chars instead of melting, buying seconds of escape time in flash fire. It does not make the wearer fireproof; it limits burn injury when every second counts. Lava heat is radiant furnace heat: basaltic lava runs 700 to 1200 C and radiates hundreds of kW/m2. Real proximity gear reflects radiant heat for short approaches; nothing wearable survives immersion. Plasma Amor Grade: tri-threat union with the plasma-amor concept layer (labeled).
grade_note: Plasma Amor Grade: tri-threat union with the plasma-amor concept layer (labeled).

details: Signature concept: JAH Amor-grade ballistic weave, a Signature-authored original layering aramid, UHMWPE, and shear-thickening interliners in one garment system.
Signature concept: plasma-amor ballistic mesh, a speculative nano-scale energy lattice; labeled Signature, not a tested product.
Signature concept: garment-wide impact sensing that maps strike location and trauma risk across the whole clothing line.
Signature concept: JAH Amor-grade flame shell, a Signature-authored original pairing PBI with a ceramic micro-layer for extended escape seconds.
Signature concept: plasma-amor thermal lattice, a speculative garment-wide heat-spreading network; labeled Signature, not a tested product.
Signature concept: garment heat mapping that reports hot spots and remaining escape-time margin across the clothing line.
specifications: Para-aramid fibers (Kevlar, Twaron): tensile strength about 3.6 GPa, density 1.44 g/cm3. A soft vest uses 20 to 35 woven layers for NIJ Level IIIA.
Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (Dyneema, Spectra): tensile strength about 3.5 GPa, density 0.97 g/cm3, so it floats. Sensitive to sustained heat above about 80 C.
NIJ 0101.06 (and the newer 0101.07): IIA stops 9 mm at 373 m/s and .40 S&W; II stops 9 mm at 398 m/s and .357 Magnum; IIIA stops 9 mm at 436 m/s and .44 Magnum.
NIJ Level III: six shots of 7.62x51 mm M80 ball at 847 m/s. Level IV: one shot of .30-06 M2 armor-piercing at 878 m/s.
